sourceEvidence.label: Librarian Slice 1 threat model, architecture, and disabled vault scaffold

assessment.summary: The evidence supports one foundational opportunity: define a single agent-owned, versioned cryptographic boundary before credential storage is enabled.

nonNegotiables: The vault agent is the only long-lived plaintext and key owner.
Master-password and recovery-key restore each work without the original device.
Windows Hello remains device-local convenience unlock.
Hostile files and unsupported versions fail closed.
Credential storage remains disabled until independent review.
assumptions: No measured latency or memory budget was supplied.
Windows 11 is the only MVP implementation and acceptance platform.
Cloud storage can replay, corrupt, delete, and observe backup metadata.
Dependency state must be refreshed when implementation begins.

opportunities.title: Establish one versioned vault cryptographic boundary
opportunities.summary: Make the agent own one explicit key hierarchy, nonce strategy, record and backup format, integrity manifest, migration policy, and review gate.
opportunities.diagnosis: The scaffold correctly disables credential storage, but later features would otherwise decide wrappers, nonces, row integrity, rollback, and migration through dispersed conventions.

evidence.claim: The threat model requires agent-owned keys, hostile-file authentication, rollback awareness, independent recovery, device-local Hello, and secret-free diagnostics.
The accepted architecture places SQLite below vault-layer authenticated encryption and blocks exact cryptography on issue #9.
The vault format exposes only ScaffoldOnly readiness and defines no credential schema or cryptographic construction.
The core explicitly reports that credential storage is not approved.
Without a single versioned specification, future unlock, record, backup, and migration paths could independently own cryptographic invariants.

desiredInvariants: One random VRK is the portable data root and every protector wraps that same root.
Master-password and recovery-key restore each work alone; Hello never becomes recovery.
Every derived key has a versioned purpose label.
Every AEAD invocation has a unique nonce under its key without timestamp or process-local state.
The authenticated manifest commits to the exact active record set.
Unknown versions, corruption, rollback, and migration failure yield no partial unlock.
Cloud storage receives one opaque authenticated backup payload.
The readiness guard remains until implementation and independent review complete.

options.title: AES-256-GCM with durable nonce counters
options.summary: Use standardized audited AES-GCM and make a crash-safe authenticated counter allocator part of every encryption path.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The hierarchy and manifest address the threat-model boundary, but nonce rollback needs a dedicated durable state machine.
It supplies an explicit format while retaining the readiness guard until review.
The core can remain disabled until the format and counter allocator are independently approved.

tradeoffs.assessment: AES-GCM is standardized and the selected Rust implementation publishes an audit, but nonce reuse would be catastrophic.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run primitive vectors and model-check counter reservation, epoch rotation, restore, and rollback.

tradeoffs.assessment: AES hardware should make record and backup encryption fast, but no Librarian benchmark exists.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark record operations and 10 MiB and 512 MiB backups on minimum Windows hardware.

tradeoffs.assessment: AEAD state is small relative to the fixed Argon2 workspace and one bounded record or backup buffer.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure peak working set during unlock, mutation, backup, and restore.

tradeoffs.assessment: Nonce safety depends on crash-consistent counter reservation across writes, migration, backup, and restored snapshots.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Terminate at every reservation and commit stage and prove no key/nonce pair can repeat.

tradeoffs.assessment: Every restore and migration requires permanent review of counter and epoch continuity.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Review all encryption call sites and document counter ownership in release checklists.

tradeoffs.assessment: Adoption or removal requires a full rewrite, and uncertain counter history cannot be reused safely.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise copy-on-write migration and downgrade with retained old encrypted artifacts.

residualRisks: Counter rollback or reuse can defeat confidentiality and integrity.
Windows Hello and rollback-anchor protection remain unresolved.

workPackages: Implement key hierarchy and strict formats.
Implement manifest, backup, rollback, migration, and vectors.
acceptanceCriteria: No repeated AES-GCM key/nonce pair is possible under crash, rollback, restore, or migration tests.
Independent review approves the exact counter state machine.
migrationNotes: Use a new key epoch and full copy-on-write rewrite.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Restore the retained pre-migration encrypted artifact; never reuse uncertain counter state.

options.title: XChaCha20-Poly1305 envelopes and encrypted manifest
options.summary: Use random 192-bit nonces, purpose-derived keys, strict record envelopes, an encrypted row-set manifest, and an outer-encrypted backup.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The hierarchy, strict parser, manifest, backup, and rollback anchor make the threat-model invariants explicit; #15 and negative tests remain required.
Cryptography and database ownership remain inside the agent boundary.
It defines the missing versioned format while keeping ScaffoldOnly until final approval.
The core continues to deny credential storage throughout implementation.

tradeoffs.assessment: Large random nonces avoid a durable allocator, the Rust crate publishes an audit statement, and the encrypted manifest authenticates the complete row set.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run RFC and published vectors, libsodium differential tests, mutation tests, fuzzing, and independent composition review.

tradeoffs.assessment: Small record operations should be inexpensive, while Argon2 and full-vault verification likely dominate unlock; no Librarian measurements exist.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure median and p95 unlock, 1/1k/10k/100k record verification, mutations, and 10 MiB/512 MiB backup.

tradeoffs.assessment: The design needs the fixed Argon2 workspace plus one bounded record or backup buffer, not a plaintext copy of the entire vault.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure peak working set and verify buffers zeroize on all exits.

tradeoffs.assessment: Random nonces remove counter reservation from the crash path; SQLite transactions and copy-on-write files contain ordinary interruption.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Crash or cancel at every commit, backup, restore, migration, and anchor-update boundary.

tradeoffs.assessment: No new service is introduced, but dependency, vector, corruption, anchor, and review evidence become release obligations.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Add dependency review, fuzz, canary, and review receipts to the release gate.

tradeoffs.assessment: The first format is new; future schema, suite, schedule, or root-key changes require explicit copy-on-write migration.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise no-op and synthetic-version migrations, interruption, readback, retained old artifact, and downgrade.

residualRisks: XChaCha20-Poly1305 is broadly deployed but not itself a final IETF RFC.
A clean device cannot prove backup freshness.
Windows Hello and rollback-anchor protection remain unresolved.
Best-effort memory erasure cannot defeat administrator or kernel access.

workPackages: Implement strict deterministic formats and secret types.
Implement key schedule, portable wrappers, records, manifest, and SQLite transactions.
Implement backup, restore, rollback anchor, and copy-on-write migration.
Run benchmarks, vectors, fuzzing, canary scans, and independent review.
acceptanceCriteria: Master-password and recovery-key clean-device restores both pass.
All primitive and complete-format vectors pass through independent verification.
All corruption, rollback, crash, migration, fuzz, and secret-canary tests pass.
A non-author reviewer approves the exact revision.
FormatReadiness remains ScaffoldOnly until the final gate.
migrationNotes: All format changes are copy-on-write with retained authenticated source artifacts.
KDF parameter changes rewrap the VRK; suite or root changes rewrite the complete vault.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Before enablement, revert code. After enablement, explicitly restore the retained pre-migration encrypted artifact and warn about post-migration data loss.

options.title: AES-256-GCM-SIV envelopes
options.summary: Keep the selected hierarchy, manifest, backup, and migration structure while using RFC 8452 misuse-resistant AEAD.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The structural design meets the same threat-model goals as the selected option, but implementation review is more demanding.
It supplies an explicit format while preserving the readiness gate.
Credential storage remains disabled until crate and composition review pass.

tradeoffs.assessment: RFC 8452 limits damage from accidental nonce reuse, but the current stable Rust crate states it has never received a security audit.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run RFC vectors, an independent implementation, and commission crate and composition review.

tradeoffs.assessment: Two-pass encryption can add CPU cost, especially for backup payloads; no product benchmark exists.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark record and 10 MiB/512 MiB backup encryption against the selected option.

tradeoffs.assessment: In-place APIs can keep memory bounded, with Argon2 still the dominant fixed workspace.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure peak working set for unlock, mutation, backup, and restore.

tradeoffs.assessment: Random nonces avoid durable counters and misuse resistance contains accidental duplicate-nonce damage better than GCM.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise deliberate duplicate-nonce fixtures plus every crash and migration boundary.

tradeoffs.assessment: The unaudited crate adds a material independent-review and monitoring obligation.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Obtain a scoped review and record crate revision, dependencies, findings, and disposition.

tradeoffs.assessment: Adoption or replacement requires a full cipher-suite rewrite even though the envelope structure is reusable.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise copy-on-write suite migration, readback, interruption, and downgrade.

residualRisks: Current stable Rust implementation lacks its own security audit.
Windows Hello and rollback-anchor protection remain unresolved.

workPackages: Implement the shared hierarchy, strict format, manifest, backup, and migration.
Validate RFC 8452 against an independent implementation.
acceptanceCriteria: Independent review covers the selected crate and complete Librarian composition.
RFC and complete-format vectors agree across independent paths.
Backup performance meets the recorded threshold.
migrationNotes: Use a new AEAD suite identifier and full copy-on-write rewrite.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Restore the retained pre-migration encrypted artifact or migrate under a newly reviewed suite.

opportunities.recommendation: Use XChaCha20-Poly1305 envelopes for the MVP because the random-nonce crash model and current independent implementation evidence best fit a small local vault; reconsider AES-GCM-SIV after equivalent review evidence exists.

openQuestions: Which Windows primitive proves the device-local, user-verification-gated Hello protector required by issue #15?
Where can the rollback anchor live with the strongest practical integrity and ACL protection?
What measured unlock latency and peak-memory thresholds define acceptable Windows UX?
Who will perform the independent review and what exact revision will it cover?
Does a future compliance target require an AES cipher suite?
